evidence.title: Lessons Learned and Iterative Enhancements: A 2-Year Experience with an Established Responsible AI Framework
evidence.outcome: Median evaluation lead time following risk-tier stratification
evidence.effect: Median evaluation lead time decreased to 9 weeks for tier 0 and 12 weeks for tier 2, compared to 20 weeks before implementation.
evidence.quote: Tier stratification reduced median evaluation lead time to 9 weeks for tier 0 and 12 weeks for tier 2, compared to 20 weeks before implementation.

commentary.bottom_line: One pre-post study without a comparison group found that risk-tier stratification shortened median AI evaluation lead time from 20 weeks to 9 weeks for tier 0 and 12 weeks for tier 2. No study measured whether scaling controls to risk changed patient harm, detection of errors in high-risk tools, or equity of outcomes, so the case for this practice rests mainly on the agreement of 29 endorsing frameworks and guidance documents.

perspectives.view: The only test is a single-site-style pre-post design with no comparator, covering 64 evaluations of 55 AI solutions. Its outcome is evaluation lead time, a process measure indirect to patient harm. Observational design, indirectness, and imprecision each lower certainty, and secular trends in review capacity could explain the change.

Median evaluation lead time fell from 20 weeks to 9 weeks for tier 0 and 12 weeks for tier 2 after tiering. This suggests tiering may free review capacity for faster handling of lower-risk tools. The study did not report staffing hours, cost, or the lead time for the highest-risk tier.

The study measured speed of review, not whether high-risk tools received stronger validation or monitoring or whether errors were caught before reaching patients. A faster review for low-tier tools also carries the risk of misclassification, and the study did not report how often tools were assigned to the wrong tier.

The study took place in a real deployment, which indicates that a tiered review process can operate within an institutional governance workflow. It did not describe fidelity to tier criteria, reviewer agreement on tier assignment, or how monitoring intensity differed by tier after go-live.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare risk-tiered governance with uniform controls using outcomes beyond review time, including safety events, detection of performance drift in high-risk tools, tier misclassification rates, governance staffing cost, and subgroup performance, ideally across several health systems with a concurrent comparison group.
commentary.underserved_note: The single test reported no data on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It is therefore unknown whether risk-tiering criteria account for harms that fall mainly on these groups, or whether tools rated low risk perform worse for them.
